benchmarks.description: The pipeline must include a workflow step that runs a dedicated secret-scanning tool (e.g., Gitleaks, TruffleHog, detect-secrets, GitGuardian/ggshield) against the source code — identified by an actual `uses:` action or `run:` command invoking one of these tools, not just a step name suggesting security. Only check for evidence within the workflow YAML files provided; do not assume GitHub's native repository-level Secret Scanning setting is enabled or disabled, since that setting is not visible in workflow files.
The pipeline must run a SAST scanner appropriate for the application language (e.g., CodeQL, Semgrep, SonarQube, Bandit) to identify security vulnerabilities in source code.

The pipeline must scan third-party dependencies and libraries against known CVEs before building or deploying the application, using a tool such as Trivy, Grype, npm audit, pip-audit, govulncheck, cargo-audit, Snyk, or OWASP Dependency-Check — identified by an actual `uses:` action or `run:` command, not a job name alone.

The pipeline must generate an SBOM (CycloneDX or SPDX format) covering the project's source-level dependencies (e.g., from package manifests like package.json, go.mod, requirements.txt) using a tool such as Syft, cdxgen, or an equivalent SBOM generator invoked via `uses:` or `run:` — evaluated independently of any SBOM generated later for build artifacts.
The pipeline must cryptographically sign the source-level SBOM (e.g., via `cosign sign` or an in-toto attestation).

The pipeline must generate a separate SBOM (CycloneDX or SPDX format) covering the produced build artifact or container image itself, using a tool such as Syft targeting the built image/artifact — evaluated independently of source-level SBOM generation.
The pipeline must cryptographically sign the build artifact SBOM using a tool such as `cosign attach-sbom` combined with `cosign sign`.

Workflow YAML files must not contain hardcoded credential values (API keys, passwords, tokens) written directly as plain text — all secret values must be referenced through the platform's secrets mechanism (e.g., `${{ secrets.* }}` in GitHub Actions) rather than embedded literally in the workflow file. This check targets the pipeline configuration files themselves, distinct from the Secret Scanning control, which targets application source code.

The pipeline must pin third-party GitHub Actions to a full-length immutable commit SHA (e.g., `uses: actions/checkout@<40-char-sha>`) rather than a mutable tag or branch reference (e.g., `@main`, `@latest`, or a movable version tag like `@v4`). A pinned major-version tag from a well-known first-party action (e.g., `actions/checkout@v4`) should be flagged as partial compliance, not full pass, unless pinned to a SHA.

The pipeline must execute build/test jobs on ephemeral, isolated runners (GitHub-hosted runners by default, or explicitly containerized self-hosted runners) rather than persistent, shared, long-lived infrastructure.

Dockerfiles and container-based build steps must reference base images by immutable digest (e.g., `FROM node:20-alpine@sha256:...`) or at minimum a specific version tag, not a floating tag such as `latest` or an untagged reference.

The pipeline must scan the final build output for known vulnerabilities before publishing or deployment. If the pipeline builds a container image, this must be a container-aware scanner (Trivy, Grype, or Clair) scanning the built image. If the pipeline produces a non-container artifact (library package, binary, tarball), an appropriate dependency/artifact scanner (Trivy in filesystem mode, npm audit, pip-audit, OWASP Dependency-Check) satisfies this control instead. Do not require both — evaluate based on what the pipeline actually builds.

The pipeline must cryptographically sign the produced artifact (container image via Cosign/Sigstore, or binary/package via GPG or platform-native signing such as npm provenance). The artifact that is signed must be the same artifact instance that was tested — evidenced by the pipeline building the artifact once and reusing that same build output (via a fixed image tag/digest or uploaded build artifact) across test, sign, and later deploy steps, rather than rebuilding it again at any later stage.

The pipeline must generate signed build provenance metadata describing how, where, and from what source commit the artifact was built (e.g., SLSA provenance via `actions/attest-build-provenance`, in-toto attestations, or `cosign attest`) — distinct from Artifact Signing, which only covers artifact integrity, not build origin.

The pipeline must scan the built artifact or container image itself (not just source code) for accidentally embedded secrets. This is distinct from source-level Secret Scanning and requires the scan to target the built output, not the repository.

The pipeline must scan Terraform, Kubernetes manifests, CloudFormation, Dockerfiles, or other infrastructure definitions for security misconfigurations using a tool such as Checkov, tfsec, KICS, or Hadolint, invoked via `uses:` or `run:`. Only applicable if the repository contains IaC/manifest files of these types.
benchmarks.applicable_only_if: repository contains Terraform, Kubernetes manifests, CloudFormation templates, or Dockerfiles

benchmarks.description: The pipeline must attack-test a running instance of the application (web UI or API) using a tool such as OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite, or Schemathesis. Evidence requires a sequence: a step that starts/deploys the application, followed by a step pointing a DAST tool at that live address — a tool reference alone without a corresponding live-target step is not sufficient. Only applicable if the project exposes an HTTP/GraphQL network surface as part of its own pipeline; not applicable to libraries, CLIs, language runtimes, or services that only consume external APIs without exposing their own.
benchmarks.applicable_only_if: the project's own CI pipeline deploys something and exposes it over a network address during the pipeline run

benchmarks.description: The pipeline must feed malformed/random input into functions that parse or process untrusted data (network input, file formats, language parsers) using a tool such as libFuzzer, AFL++, go-fuzz, jsfuzz, or OSS-Fuzz/ClusterFuzzLite integration — evidenced by a `fuzz/` or `test/fuzzers/` directory, OSS-Fuzz config files, or a workflow step invoking a fuzzing binary. Distinct from DAST: applicable regardless of whether the project exposes a network endpoint.

Workflow tokens must follow least privilege: top-level `permissions:` should default to read-only (`contents: read` or equivalent minimal scope), with any required write access declared explicitly at the job level, scoped only to what that specific job needs. Flag workflows missing a `permissions:` block entirely or setting `permissions: write-all` at either level.

Before deploying to any live environment (staging or production), the pipeline must verify the artifact's signature (e.g., `cosign verify`) against a trusted public key. This is a re-verification of a signature created earlier at build time, not a new signing operation.
Before deploying to any live environment, the pipeline must verify the artifact's build provenance attestation matches the expected source repository and commit.

benchmarks.control: Dangerous Workflow Trigger + Untrusted Checkout Combination
benchmarks.description: No workflow may combine a privileged trigger (`pull_request_target` or `workflow_run`) with an explicit checkout of the pull request's head code (e.g., `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`) within the same job. `pull_request_target` alone — without an explicit PR-head checkout in the same job — is a common, legitimate pattern (auto-labeling, PR comments, stale-issue bots) and must not be flagged on its own. A job gated with `if: github.event.label.name == ...` should be treated as reduced risk, not full failure.

benchmarks.control: Script Injection via Untrusted Context Variables
benchmarks.description: No `run:` step may directly interpolate a user-controllable GitHub context value (e.g., `github.event.pull_request.title`, `github.event.issue.body`, `github.event.comment.body`, `github.head_ref`) into an inline shell command string — including on the unprivileged `pull_request` trigger. The safe equivalent passes the same value via an `env:` block instead of inline interpolation.
